Let’s talk about something that holds so many people back—often without them even realizing it.
The Cost of Reluctance to Claim Achievements—and the Power of Self-Advocacy.
Have you ever found yourself staying quiet about your hard work, hoping someone would just notice? It happens all the time, and it usually starts early on, when we’re taught to be humble and not draw too much attention to ourselves.
But here’s the thing: in the workplace, if you aren’t comfortable talking about what you’ve accomplished, it’s easy to get overlooked.
Picture this. Your team just wrapped up a big project. Some folks are quick to share what they did, while others sit back, thinking their results will speak for themselves. But the truth is, the people who consistently talk about their contributions are the ones who get noticed—and usually, they’re first in line for new opportunities.
Now, this isn’t just about one group or another, but for many women, the pressure to avoid self-promotion can feel even stronger. There’s this worry: “If I speak up about what I’ve done, will people think I’m bragging?” So, instead, they brush off compliments or shift credit to others.
While that might feel polite, it actually comes at a cost. Because in most workplaces, out of sight really does mean out of mind. Leaders are busy. They can’t see everything that’s happening. If you want to be considered for that next project or a raise, you need to make your achievements visible.
Here’s something to consider: what if sharing your accomplishments wasn’t about bragging, but simply about clear communication? Think of it as giving people the information they need to make good decisions about you. It’s also a way to show confidence, which encourages others to do the same.
So, how can you get better at this?
Try keeping a running list of your wins and contributions. That way, when it’s time to talk about them, you’ve got real examples at your fingertips.
Practice stating your achievements briefly and factually—focus on what changed because of your work.
Ask for feedback from people you trust, so you get a clearer picture of your strengths and what you could improve.
And maybe most importantly, start seeing self-advocacy as a way to lift up your whole team. When you highlight the value you bring, you’re also shining a light on the group’s success.
Step by step, these habits can help you feel more comfortable sharing your achievements—and over time, you’ll help create a workplace culture where everyone’s contributions are truly seen and valued.
And there’s even more to it. When you’re able to talk confidently about your successes, it shapes how others see your leadership potential. People start to see you as someone who’s ready for bigger challenges and more responsibility.
That’s how new doors open—both for you and for those who follow your example.
